title: An Analysis of Nigeria’s Economy
text:
Nigeria through the years has experienced periods of political instability due to civil wars, and poor implementation of economic policy (Marwah 2020) that resulted in the nation’s wildly fluctuating GDP per capita. Since 1950 to 2024, Nigeria’s per capita growth has risen 322.5% from US$1,200 to US$5070 with an average annual growth rate of 1.97% over the period (Bolt and Zanden 2023) , which is a significant increase but filled extreme downturns. To better understand Nigeria’s economic performance, we will examine the per capita GDP growth adjusted by purchasing power parity (PPP) from the 1950s and view its stagnation over the years as a product of governmental economic mismanagement.


Code
ggplot(
    nigeria_data, aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color='blue') +
        geom_point(stat = "summary", color = "black") +
        geom_point(
            data = subset(nigeria_data, Year %in% c(1968, 1977, 2015)),
            aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`),
            color = "red",size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 15) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria's GDP per capita, 2011 international US$",
    subtitle = "Used Maddison Project Database (2023). Constant 2011 international dollars (PPP-adjusted).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP per capita",
    caption = "Source: Maddison Project Database (2023) | ourworldindata.org"
  )









Since 1950, Nigeria’s GDP per capita has experienced several fluctuations with a trough that had a steady climb afterward, and two major peaks followed by declines in 1968, 1977, and 2015 (Bolt and Zanden 2023). By 1968, GDP per capita had fallen 7.17% from 1950 and 14.8% from her independence year of 1960 marking the nations lowest recorded per capita GDP (Bolt and Zanden 2023). While after this period, Nigeria saw significant prosperity in the rise that followed it, but the period before was marked by a constant shift in governing bodies due to the independence shift, coups and civil wars that redecided due to humanitarian action from foreign parties by 1968(Mullenbach 2016). By 1977 Nigeria had established itself as an oil exporting nation and had seen a boom in nominal output according to Pinto, 1987, while the GDP per capita since 1968 rose by 99.3% (Bolt and Zanden 2023). However a downturn followed and despite a stable government, it heavily invested in oil exports without much other fiscal infrastructure and leaving the nation vulnerable to shocks in the oil market such as in 1978 which saw an 8.65% drop in GDP per capita from the previous year (Pinto 1987). Finally, by 2015 per capita GDP had grown an astounding 150.4% since 1977 and 257.2% since 1987 which was the last significant drop. This period saw the most consistent growth in per capita for Nigeria largely due to oil exporting, and a rebasing of the value rather than an impactful improvement in the output per person (Ohuocha 2014). These three points reflect an economy that is too dependent on the volatile market of oil, political uncertainty, and the false appearance of real growth, all are due to government mismanagement.


Code
ggplot(
    gdpMaddison, aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`,color = `Country`)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = gdpMaddison %>% group_by(`Country`) %>% filter(Year == max(Year)),
    aes(label = `Country`),
    hjust = 0,
    direction = "y",
    nudge_x = 2,
    size = 5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 15) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP per capita, 2011 international US$",
    subtitle = "Used Maddison Project Database (2023). Constant 2011 international dollars (PPP-adjusted).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP per capita",
    caption = "Source: Maddison Project Database (2023) | ourworldindata.org"
  )









Comparing Nigeria to other oil exporting nations brings up two important points; Nigeria is the largest exporter of crude oil in Africa (Eregha and Mesagan 2020) and experiences one of the greater declines in per capita GDP(Bolt and Zanden 2023). Nations such as Algeria, Angola and Libya are oil exporting much like Nigeria and would experience shocks in their markets just as much. Findings from Eregha and Mesagan (2020) conclude that other nations per capita growth benefits from oil production while Nigeria does not due poor resource management on the institutions’ part. Algeria, Angola, and Libya have been much more advantageous in their per capita growth since 1950. Algeria grew 520.7% with an average annual growth rate of 2.5%, Angola grew 264.9% with an average annual growth rate of 1.76%, and Libya grew 1957.3% with an average annual growth rate of 4.17% (Bolt and Zanden 2023). Compared with Nigeria’s 322.5% growth with an average annual growth rate of 1.97%, Angola seems to fair worse but will begin passing Nigeria due to better efforts of resource management and without Nigeria’s dependence on exporting oil without investment in other industries (Eregha and Mesagan 2020). Additionally, Nigeria in comparison suffers in managing policy to benefit its most abundant resource, which in turn negatively influences per capita GDP and the overall living standard. Because of poor government policies, Nigeria can continue to grow its per capita GDP, but it will do so at the mercy of the oil markets until investment in other sectors occur and the populus finds confidence in the government.
We looked at the trend which was affected by global oil prices, shifts in governing bodies that instill uncertainty and re-evaluations of economic financing that give false hope for the growth, while focusing on oil negatively affects the nation’s per capita growth. Nigeria does continue to grow its per capita GDP, but it is too closely tied to the oil market, and this inherently means the standard of living with always depend on it. When a nation solely specialises in a single industry such as oil it forgets its agriculture and manufacturing and must import these to compensate. In Nigeria’s case, these imports will be less accessible when oil negatively impacts per capita GDP, and further decline can occur. Thus, the nations governing body needs better policies and better political infrastructure to avoid the current trajectory.

title: An Analysis of Nigeria’s Economy
text:
The accumulation of capital within a nation can be closely tied to its economic growth using the Solow model (Solow 1956). Thus, we will look at Nigeria’s history of capital accumulation with available data from 2013 to 2023 using gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in current (2023) US$ standard as an indicator. View its share with the nation’s gross domestic product (GDP) compared to world averages and look at the trajectory of economic growth with the ideas of the Solow model.


Code
ggplot(
    capdt, aes(x = year, y = GFCFcurrentUS)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color='orange') +
        geom_point(stat = "summary", color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
  labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
  breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10)
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria's Gross Fixed Capital Formation (Current US$)",
    subtitle = "Gross Fixed Capital Formation (Current US$) (WEO).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Gross Fixed Capital Formation",
    caption = "Source: African Development Bank Group (2023) | dataportal.afdb.org"
  )









Nigeria’s GFCF between 2013 to 2023 has been fluctuating with a 36.8% increase from US$72.9B to US$99.7B, averaging a 3.17% annual change (African Development Bank Group 2023). In between this period, there was a peak in 2014, where GFCF rose to US$85.7B from the previous year as the country saw further production in its oil industry and governmental policies to expand this sector (African Development Bank Group 2023; Lee 2014). However, by 2018, GFCF had dropped 38% to US$53.1B, marking a significant trough as reduced investment constrained their productive capacity with a growing population (African Development Bank Group 2023; Lee 2014). Since then, GFCF has shown a consistent recovery, reaching US$99.7B by 2023 (African Development Bank Group 2023).


Code
ggplot(
    GFCFperGDP_combined, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cap_pct_gdp, color = "World"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cap_pct_gdp), size = 2.5, color = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(y = GFCFperGDP, color = "Nigeria"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = GFCFperGDP),color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria Vs. World Gross Fixed Capital Formation (% GDP)",
    subtitle = "Nigeria's and the World's Gross Fixed Capital Formation as a Percantage of GDP (WEO).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "% of GDP",
    caption = "Source: African Development Bank Group (2023) & World Bank Group | dataportal.afdb.org & data.worldbank.org"
  )









At 16.1%, Nigeria’s share of GFCF in GDP is 1.6 times below the world’s average of 26.3%, although significantly greater, the world average increases at 0.39% while Nigeria increases at 6.96% annually (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). Nigeria’s share of GFCF rose from 13.9% to 27.4%, remaining stagnant until 2018 when it fell to its lowest of 12.6%, while the world rose to 26.5% (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). Post 2018, Nigeria’s share climbed to its highest peak of 27.4% by 2023, corresponding with the increase in GFCF that surpassed the world average of 26.5% in the same year (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). The trajectory of Nigeria’s share has seen recent increases at a larger rate, while the global average saw a small decline at lower rates, highlighting the nation’s aim for growth.
According to the Solow model, increases in capital will contribute to increases in productivity, which increases per capita GDP (Solow 1956). In Nigeria’s case, the opposite occurs, where in our period there is an increase in GFCF, but GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) falls according to Bolt and Zanden (2023). GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) fell 5.34% while GFCF and its share increased (African Development Bank Group 2023; Bolt and Zanden 2023). This prevents us from aligning the country with the model, as per capita GDP (PPPadjusted) does not trend with capital formation. However, Nigeria’s share of GFCF as a percentage of GDP at PPP fell by 8.61% in the available data between 2013 and 2019, which follows the same decline for per capita GDP (PPP-adjusted), and its share (University of Groningen and University of California, Davis 2019). Applying the model when comparing GFCF and its share to per capita GDP (PPP-adjusted) yields unapplicable results, but when GFCF’s share is PPP-adjusted, we can find evidence of the model working to predict growth.
In the period from 2013 to 2023, Nigeria’s capital accumulation has significantly expanded, going beyond world averages, indicating an increase in the nation’s physical and monetary capital with the aim of improving its growth. Additionally, increased gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and its share of GDP have not yielded a similar trend in GDP per capita, but it does follow the share of GFCF as a percentage of GDP at PPP, as predicted in the Solow model.

title: An Analysis of Nigeria’s Economy
text:
Nigeria’s human capital is generally perceived as subpar, with a high population of 237.5 million; there is potential for the nation to benefit in human productivity (Statista 2025). According to the World Bank Group, 2023, Human Capital Index (HCI) is the productivity of an individual by the age of 18, with their education, skills and health. This report examines Nigeria’s current efforts in education and the resulting workforce to assess the nation’s position in managing and developing its human capital.





Although Nigeria has a population advantage, it underperforms in HCI inputs. By 2024, Nigeria’s HCI reached 0.42, indicating that Nigerians born that year will be 42% productive by age 18, while the world average is 0.65, ranking Nigeria 163rd in the world (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA) 2024). Additionally, the average years of schooling in Nigeria is 7.2 while the world’s is 8.9, resulting in adult literacy rates of 62% in the country and 87.3% worldwide (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA) 2024). Nigeria falls behind in cultivating productive individuals compared to the world standards, and this shows that challenges are hindering it from leveraging its human capital.
Education is a key component of HCI, and in 2025, Nigeria will spend 7% of its fiscal budget on education, well below UNESCO’s recommendation of 15% to 20% (Shehu and Onunwa 2025). Due to lower funding in this sector, Nigeria experiences shortages of school supplies and teachers, which prevent students from continuing their schooling and lead to fewer education years (Shehu and Onunwa 2025). However, there are foreign parties such as the World Bank Group that have committed to providing additional funds for Nigeria’s educational sector through the “HOPE-EDU program,” which will donate US$500 million (Nasir and Laushi 2025). Although the nation struggles to prioritise adolescent skills, its trajectory for growth could improve if its governance leverages external aid to its advantage.
While Nigeria works to improve its educational investment, its adult literacy rate remains low at 62% due to a poor educational system, with an additional discrepancy of a 20.4% difference between men and women in 2021 (Countryeconomy.com 2024). This impact is seen in the workforce’s productivity, as the nation faces a surplus of skilled and low-skilled individuals who cannot acquire further skills (World Bank 2025). The major gap between genders highlights the inequality in education, where women face barriers to entering the workforce or improving their skills. With less emphasis on women’s contributions, Nigeria’s growth potential is stagnated by a low-skilled workforce.
Nigeria is a nation that can leverage its large population to increase productivity; however, it faces shortcomings in producing individuals who can contribute to its economic growth. Weakened by a poor education system, many adults lack the necessary skills for efficient work, with women being sidelined. The nation’s low HCI is a culmination of these facts, but with aid and adequate institutions, this can be improved.

title: An Analysis of Nigeria’s Economy
text:
Nigeria’s financial system is a mixture of traditional formal banking and informal nonregulated services, according to the Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) (2024). While there is a variety of options, wealth gaps and gender inequality persist, which leave many financially excluded. According to the World Bank Group (2023), the financial inclusion rate is the percentage of adults who have access to formal or informal financial services. This report examines Nigeria’s financial exclusion and inclusion, how its population fares in this state and how its government addresses the issues.





The Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) (2024) credits formal bank market competition, increased mobile phone usage and urbanisation for affecting financial access in Nigeria. This has led to 64% of adult Nigerians being formally financially included and 74% with the additional informal means by 2023 (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). This is an increase from 68% in 2020, resulting in fewer people being financially excluded (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Although only 26% of adult Nigerians are financially excluded, this still accounts for 28.9 million people, mostly in rural areas and dependents such as women (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024).
As a result, Nigerians, many of whom live in the northern parts of the country, face barriers to financial well-being due to limited accessibility (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). While only 17% of urban residents are excluded, 37% of rural residents are excluded, which was a 2% increase from 35% in 2020, despite the national increase in services (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Due to increased urbanisation in Nigeria, formal banking services focus their attention on urban cities, ignoring rural areas, and this is evident in the agricultural sector, where small businesses face high barriers to accessing formal start-up funds (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Due to a lack of formal services, informal services, which include connections and high-interest credit providers, are heavily relied on to provide financial needs (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024).
To address these issues, the Central Bank of Nigeria implemented the National Financial Inclusion Strategy in 2012, which aimed to reduce the exclusion rate to 20% by 2020. Despite not reaching the target, the exclusion rate is 26% by 2023, a significant decrease from 40% when the policy was first enacted (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). This was achieved through incentivizing competition in the banking sector to bring in a wider range of services, providing infrastructure in telecommunications to increase mobile phone usage for digital financial offerings and introducing services for dependents like women through micro-financing (Central Bank of Nigeria).
Nigeria’s mixed financial sector shows considerable promise, as evidenced by its progress in expanding financial accessibility through policy. There is an incentive for competition in the financial and technology sectors that aid financial inclusion. However, dependents such as women and rural residents continue to be excluded, which shows areas where improvement is needed.

title: Federal Fiscal Data
text:
Statement of Operations
Statistics Canada (2018)’s definition of the statement of operations is: “summarises the transactions in revenue, expense, net investment in non-financial assets, net acquisition of financial assets and net incurrence of liabilities”. This gives us the general view of revenues and expenses, whose difference results in the net operating balance.
Revenue consists of: taxes on income, profits, capital gains, payroll, property, goods and services, international transactions and other tax bases, social contributions, grants from other levels of government, property income such as interest on loans and distributed income of government business enterprises and some other types of revenue. (Statistics Canada 2018)
Expenses consist of: compensation paid to employees, purchases of goods and services, subsidies, interest on public debt, social benefits paid, consumption of fixed capital and some other types of expenses. (Statistics Canada 2018)








Variable
Description




Net operating balance
“is a summary measure of the ongoing sustainability of the government operations. Net operating balance equals total revenues less total expenses.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Revenue
“refers to the gross inflow of economic benefits or service potential during the reporting period when those inflows result in an increase in equity, other than increases relating to contributions from owners.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Taxes
“compulsory, unrequited amounts receivable by government units from individual institutional units.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: taxes on income, profits and capital gains, taxes on payroll and workforce, taxes on property, taxes on goods and services (value added tax such as GST and HST), and other taxes


Taxes on income, profits and capital gains
“are levied on the actual or presumptive net income of individuals, on the profits of corporations and enterprises, and on capital gains, whether realized or not, on land, securities, and other assets. Intragovernmental payments are eliminated in consolidation.” (World Bank 2026)
It is the sum of federal, provincial and territorial income, profits and capital gains taxes received during the reference period. (Statistics Canada 2021)


Taxes on payroll and workforce
Tax income received from taxes on employment wages and salaries.
“Taxes on payroll and workforce are not of major importance in Canada, in part because they provide a disincentive for employment.” (Statistics Canada 2018)


Taxes on property
“Tax income received from taxes on property owned, are most significant for local government administrations.” (Statistics Canada 2018)
Includes: recurrent taxes on immovable property (land, buildings and other structures) or net wealth, special assessments, business property taxes, payments in lieu of taxes and non-recurrent taxes on property such as estate, inheritance and gift taxes. (Statistics Canada 2018)


Taxes on goods and services
“taxes that become payable as a result of the production, sale, transfer, leasing, or delivery of goods and rendering of services, or as a result of their use for own consumption, or own capital formation.” (Statistics Canada 2018)
Includes: goods and services tax (GST), the harmonized sales tax (HST), the retail sales tax, excise taxes primarily on liquor, tobacco and gasoline, and taxes on specific services such as air travel, taxes on permission to use goods, such as motor vehicle licences, or to perform activities, as well as the profits of fiscal monopolies. (Statistics Canada 2018)


Other taxes
Includes: taxes on international trade and transactions consist mainly of Customs and other import duties. (Statistics Canada 2018)


Social contributions
“Social contributions are actual or imputed revenue receivable by social insurance schemes to make provision for social insurance benefits payable. Social contributions differ from taxes in that the contributor secures the right to an entitlement when certain conditions arise, such as the loss of employment.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: Employment Insurance Program, Canada and Quebec Pension Plan premiums


Grants, revenue
“Grants are transfers receivable by government units from other resident or non-resident government units or international organizations, and that do not meet the definition of a tax, subsidy or social contribution. The grants can be current or capital and can be receivable in cash or in kind.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: Federal government health transfers, Federal government equalization payments, Provincial and territorial governments transfers to health and education institutions, Transfers to municipalities for infrastructures. (Statistics Canada 2014)


Other revenue
“Other revenue represents all revenue receivable excluding taxes, social contributions and grants.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Can include: property income such as interest income, royalties, dividends, and remitted profits of government business enterprises, Sales of goods and services, Fines, penalties, and forfeits, Voluntary transfers other than grants, Miscellaneous and unidentified revenue, interest income on bonds, natural resource royalty fees, profits from government business enterprises. (Statistics Canada 2014)


Property income
Under other revenue, consists of interest income, royalties, dividends, and remitted profits of government business enterprises of property. (Statistics Canada 2014)


Sales of goods and services
Under other revenue, consists of revenue received from the sale of goods and services from government businesses


Fines, penalties and forfeits
Under other revenue, consists of revenue received from fines, penalties and forfeits


Voluntary transfers other than grants
Under other revenue, consists of revenue received from voluntary transfers other than grants


Miscellaneous revenue
Under other revenue, consists of auto insurance premiums, drug plan premiums and revenue not elsewhere classified. (Statistics Canada 2024)


Expense
“refers to the decrease in economic benefits or service potential, during the reporting period, in the form of outflows or consumption of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decreases in equity, other than those relating to distributions to owners.” Statistics Canada (2024)


Compensation of employees
“Compensation of employees is the total remuneration, in cash or in kind, payable to a government employee in return for work done during the accounting period, except for work connected with own account capital formation.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: wages, salaries and employer’s social contributions which can be pensions and other retirement benefits


Use of goods and services
“This category consists of goods and services used for the production of market and nonmarket goods and services—except for own-account capital formation—plus goods purchased for resale less the net change in inventories of work in progress, finished goods, and goods held for resale.” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: payments made to contractors, utilities and telecommunications, and others such as building maintenance.


Consumption of fixed capital
“Consumption of fixed capital is the decline, during the course of an accounting period, in the current value of the stock of fixed assets owned and used by a general government unit as a result of physical deterioration, normal obsolescence, or normal accidental damage.” (Statistics Canada 2014)


Interest expense
“Interest is payable by units that incur liabilities by borrowing funds from another unit. Interest is the expense that the debtor unit incurs for the use of the principal outstanding, which represents the economic value that has been provided by the creditor” (Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: interest payable on financial assets such a SDRs, deposits, debt securities, loans, and other accounts


Subsidies
“Subsidies are current unrequited transfers that government units make to enterprises on the basis of the level of their production activities or the quantities or values of the goods or services they produce, sell, export, or import.
Subsidies may be designed to influence levels of production, the prices at which outputs are sold, or the remuneration of the enterprises. Subsidies are payable to producers only, not to final consumers.” Statistics Canada (2014)
Includes: Direct foreign trade subsidies, Subsidies payable to resident producers, Subsidies on payroll or workforce


Grants, expense
Under expenses, consists of grants paid to others


Social benefits
“Social benefits are current transfers, in cash or in kind, receivable by households intended to provide for the needs that arise from social risks, such as sickness, unemployment, retirement, housing or education. These benefits are paid by a government unit to protect the entire population or specific segments of it against certain social risks. Social risks are events or circumstances that may adversely affect the welfare of households.” Statistics Canada (2014)
Includes: Employment insurance program, Canada and Quebec Pension Plan, Child care benefits, Drug plans, Workers’ compensation boards benefits, Goods and Services Tax (GST) credits


Other expense
“Other expense is a broad category that includes government expenses other than those listed above. Generally these types of expenses are incurred by government business enterprises.”(Statistics Canada 2014)
Includes: property expense other than interest such as dividends payable, payments for the lease of land or payments for the extraction of minerals or fossil fuels, transfers by government to persons (other than social benefits) and non-profit institutions serving households. (Statistics Canada 2014)

title: Federal Fiscal Data
text:
Statement of Financial Position
Statistics Canada (2024)’s definition of the statement of financial position/balance sheet is: “records the stocks of assets, liabilities, and the net worth for each accounting period”. That being, the total value of the assets always equals the total value of the liabilities plus net worth (Statistics Canada 2018).
Assets consist of: Nonfinancial assets, Financial assets, Currency and deposits assets, Debt securities assets, Loans assets, Equity and investment fund shares assets, Insurance and pension assets, Other accounts receivable. (Statistics Canada 2018)
Liabilities consist of: Currency and deposits liabilities, Debt securities liabilities, Loans liabilities, Equity and investment fund shares liabilities, Insurance and pension and standardized guarantee schemes liabilities, Other accounts payable, Monetary gold and special drawing rights (SDR) liabilities. (Statistics Canada 2018)








Variable
Description




Net worth
“is defined as the total assets less total liabilities and is an important measure for assessing the sustainability of fiscal activities. The balance sheet components include domestic and foreign counterparts.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Net financial worth
“The net financial worth position equals total stock of financial assets minus liabilities.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Nonfinancial assets
“refers to assets that are produced (e.g. machinery and equipment) or non-produced (e.g. land and natural resources). These assets represent the produced and natural capital that companies use to generate income.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Financial assets
“refers to all financial claims, shares or other equity in corporations plus gold bullion held by monetary authorities as a reserve asset.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Currency and deposits, assets
“This represents the net acquisition of currency and deposits by government units within a given accounting period. For domestic currency this represents the change in the stock of currency and deposits between the opening balance sheet and the closing balance sheet. For foreign currency and deposits, this represents the change in the stock of foreign currency and deposits less any change in value resulting from changes in the exchange rate between the domestic currency and the foreign currency” (Statistics Canada 2014)


Debt securities, assets
“Debt securities are negotiable financial instruments serving as evidence of a debt and for which there normally exist a schedule of interest payments and principal repayment” (Statistics Canada 2014)


Loans, assets
“A loan is a financial instrument that is created when a creditor lends funds directly to a debtor. If a loan is tradable, it is reclassified to debt securities.” Statistics Canada (2014)


Equity and investment fund shares, assets
“Equity and investment fund shares have the distinguishing feature that the holders own a residual claim on the assets of the unit that issued the instrument. In contrast to debt securities, equity does not generally provide the owner with a right to a pre-determined amount or an amount determined according to a fixed formula. Government units themselves cannot issue shares but they can hold shares of other units. Shares and other equity are usually evidenced by shares, stocks or participations.” Statistics Canada (2014)


Insurance and pension, assets
“This category consists of nonlife insurance technical reserves, life insurance and annuities entitlements, pension entitlements, and claims of pension funds on pension manager. These represent assets of a public sector unit as the insurer, pension fund, and a corresponding asset of the policyholder or beneficiaries (most commonly households)” Statistics Canada (2014)


Other accounts receivable
“This represents the value of trade credit and advances and miscellaneous items that either need to be paid or are due to be received by public sector units.” (Statistics Canada 2014)


Liabilities
“refers to the present obligations of the entity arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow from the entity of resources embodying economic benefits or service potential.” (Statistics Canada 2024)


Currency and deposits, liabilities
Currency and deposits owing to others.


Debt securities, liabilities
Debt securities owing to others.


Loans, liabilities
Loans owing to others.


Insurance, pension and standardized guarantee schemes, liabilities
“This category consists of nonlife insurance technical reserves, life insurance and annuities entitlements, pension entitlements, claims of pension funds on pension manager, and provision for calls under standardized guarantee schemes (such as student loans guarantees and deposit insurance guarantees).
These represent liabilities of a public sector unit as the insurer, pension fund, or issuer of standardized guarantees and a corresponding asset of the policyholder or beneficiaries (most commonly households).” (Statistics Canada 2014)


Other accounts payable
Amounts owing to others.


Monetary gold and special drawing rights (SDR), liabilities
“Monetary gold is gold to which the monetary authorities have title and is held as a reserve asset.
Special drawing rights (SDRs) are international reserve assets created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and allocated to its members to supplement existing reserve asset. An SDR represents an unconditional right to obtain foreign exchange or other reserve assets from other IMF countries.” (Statistics Canada 2014)

title: An Analysis of Nigeria’s Economy
text:
Nigeria is one of the most prominent countries in Western Africa, known for its rich history in cultural diversity and abundant natural resources. Despite this, the nation’s development is stained with exploitation and corruption by its government. As a former British colony, Nigeria had to grow as an independent nation and rise above its own exploitation of its people; however, its governance has been hindered by persistent political instability. To examine the effect of Nigeria’s institutions, we will look at aspects that constitute the economic growth of a nation: GDP per capita, physical-capital accumulation, human-capital accumulation and its financial inclusion. Through these aspects, we see Nigeria as a nation with potential for growth driven by its abundant human resources and financial innovation but stagnating due to limited action from the government.


Nigeria through the years has experienced periods of political instability due to civil wars, and poor implementation of economic policy (Marwah 2020) that resulted in the nation’s wildly fluctuating GDP per capita. Since 1950 to 2024, Nigeria’s per capita growth has risen 322.5% from US$1,200 to US$5070 with an average annual growth rate of 1.97% over the period (Bolt and Zanden 2023) , which is a significant increase but filled extreme downturns. To better understand Nigeria’s economic performance, we will examine the per capita GDP growth adjusted by purchasing power parity (PPP) from the 1950s and view its stagnation over the years as a product of governmental economic mismanagement.


Code
ggplot(
    nigeria_data, aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color='blue') +
        geom_point(stat = "summary", color = "black") +
        geom_point(
            data = subset(nigeria_data, Year %in% c(1968, 1977, 2015)),
            aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`),
            color = "red",size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 15) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria's GDP per capita, 2011 international US$",
    subtitle = "Used Maddison Project Database (2023). Constant 2011 international dollars (PPP-adjusted).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP per capita",
    caption = "Source: Maddison Project Database (2023) | ourworldindata.org"
  )









Since 1950, Nigeria’s GDP per capita has experienced several fluctuations with a trough that had a steady climb afterward, and two major peaks followed by declines in 1968, 1977, and 2015 (Bolt and Zanden 2023). By 1968, GDP per capita had fallen 7.17% from 1950 and 14.8% from her independence year of 1960 marking the nations lowest recorded per capita GDP (Bolt and Zanden 2023). While after this period, Nigeria saw significant prosperity in the rise that followed it, but the period before was marked by a constant shift in governing bodies due to the independence shift, coups and civil wars that redecided due to humanitarian action from foreign parties by 1968(Mullenbach 2016). By 1977 Nigeria had established itself as an oil exporting nation and had seen a boom in nominal output according to Pinto, 1987, while the GDP per capita since 1968 rose by 99.3% (Bolt and Zanden 2023). However a downturn followed and despite a stable government, it heavily invested in oil exports without much other fiscal infrastructure and leaving the nation vulnerable to shocks in the oil market such as in 1978 which saw an 8.65% drop in GDP per capita from the previous year (Pinto 1987). Finally, by 2015 per capita GDP had grown an astounding 150.4% since 1977 and 257.2% since 1987 which was the last significant drop. This period saw the most consistent growth in per capita for Nigeria largely due to oil exporting, and a rebasing of the value rather than an impactful improvement in the output per person (Ohuocha 2014). These three points reflect an economy that is too dependent on the volatile market of oil, political uncertainty, and the false appearance of real growth, all are due to government mismanagement.


Code
ggplot(
    gdpMaddison, aes(x = Year, y = `GDP per capita_PPP`,color = `Country`)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = gdpMaddison %>% group_by(`Country`) %>% filter(Year == max(Year)),
    aes(label = `Country`),
    hjust = 0,
    direction = "y",
    nudge_x = 2,
    size = 5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 15) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP per capita, 2011 international US$",
    subtitle = "Used Maddison Project Database (2023). Constant 2011 international dollars (PPP-adjusted).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP per capita",
    caption = "Source: Maddison Project Database (2023) | ourworldindata.org"
  )









Comparing Nigeria to other oil exporting nations brings up two important points; Nigeria is the largest exporter of crude oil in Africa (Eregha and Mesagan 2020) and experiences one of the greater declines in per capita GDP(Bolt and Zanden 2023). Nations such as Algeria, Angola and Libya are oil exporting much like Nigeria and would experience shocks in their markets just as much. Findings from Eregha and Mesagan (2020) conclude that other nations per capita growth benefits from oil production while Nigeria does not due poor resource management on the institutions’ part. Algeria, Angola, and Libya have been much more advantageous in their per capita growth since 1950. Algeria grew 520.7% with an average annual growth rate of 2.5%, Angola grew 264.9% with an average annual growth rate of 1.76%, and Libya grew 1957.3% with an average annual growth rate of 4.17% (Bolt and Zanden 2023). Compared with Nigeria’s 322.5% growth with an average annual growth rate of 1.97%, Angola seems to fair worse but will begin passing Nigeria due to better efforts of resource management and without Nigeria’s dependence on exporting oil without investment in other industries (Eregha and Mesagan 2020). Additionally, Nigeria in comparison suffers in managing policy to benefit its most abundant resource, which in turn negatively influences per capita GDP and the overall living standard. Because of poor government policies, Nigeria can continue to grow its per capita GDP, but it will do so at the mercy of the oil markets until investment in other sectors occur and the populus finds confidence in the government.
We looked at the trend which was affected by global oil prices, shifts in governing bodies that instill uncertainty and re-evaluations of economic financing that give false hope for the growth, while focusing on oil negatively affects the nation’s per capita growth. Nigeria does continue to grow its per capita GDP, but it is too closely tied to the oil market, and this inherently means the standard of living with always depend on it. When a nation solely specialises in a single industry such as oil it forgets its agriculture and manufacturing and must import these to compensate. In Nigeria’s case, these imports will be less accessible when oil negatively impacts per capita GDP, and further decline can occur. Thus, the nations governing body needs better policies and better political infrastructure to avoid the current trajectory.



The accumulation of capital within a nation can be closely tied to its economic growth using the Solow model (Solow 1956). Thus, we will look at Nigeria’s history of capital accumulation with available data from 2013 to 2023 using gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in current (2023) US$ standard as an indicator. View its share with the nation’s gross domestic product (GDP) compared to world averages and look at the trajectory of economic growth with the ideas of the Solow model.


Code
ggplot(
    capdt, aes(x = year, y = GFCFcurrentUS)) +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color='orange') +
        geom_point(stat = "summary", color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
  labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
  breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10)
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria's Gross Fixed Capital Formation (Current US$)",
    subtitle = "Gross Fixed Capital Formation (Current US$) (WEO).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Gross Fixed Capital Formation",
    caption = "Source: African Development Bank Group (2023) | dataportal.afdb.org"
  )









Nigeria’s GFCF between 2013 to 2023 has been fluctuating with a 36.8% increase from US$72.9B to US$99.7B, averaging a 3.17% annual change (African Development Bank Group 2023). In between this period, there was a peak in 2014, where GFCF rose to US$85.7B from the previous year as the country saw further production in its oil industry and governmental policies to expand this sector (African Development Bank Group 2023; Lee 2014). However, by 2018, GFCF had dropped 38% to US$53.1B, marking a significant trough as reduced investment constrained their productive capacity with a growing population (African Development Bank Group 2023; Lee 2014). Since then, GFCF has shown a consistent recovery, reaching US$99.7B by 2023 (African Development Bank Group 2023).


Code
ggplot(
    GFCFperGDP_combined, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cap_pct_gdp, color = "World"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cap_pct_gdp), size = 2.5, color = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(y = GFCFperGDP, color = "Nigeria"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = GFCFperGDP),color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1)),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10) 
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::comma,                   
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 20)    
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray85"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray40"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Nigeria Vs. World Gross Fixed Capital Formation (% GDP)",
    subtitle = "Nigeria's and the World's Gross Fixed Capital Formation as a Percantage of GDP (WEO).",
    x = "Year",
    y = "% of GDP",
    caption = "Source: African Development Bank Group (2023) & World Bank Group | dataportal.afdb.org & data.worldbank.org"
  )









At 16.1%, Nigeria’s share of GFCF in GDP is 1.6 times below the world’s average of 26.3%, although significantly greater, the world average increases at 0.39% while Nigeria increases at 6.96% annually (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). Nigeria’s share of GFCF rose from 13.9% to 27.4%, remaining stagnant until 2018 when it fell to its lowest of 12.6%, while the world rose to 26.5% (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). Post 2018, Nigeria’s share climbed to its highest peak of 27.4% by 2023, corresponding with the increase in GFCF that surpassed the world average of 26.5% in the same year (World Bank 2025; African Development Bank Group 2023). The trajectory of Nigeria’s share has seen recent increases at a larger rate, while the global average saw a small decline at lower rates, highlighting the nation’s aim for growth.
According to the Solow model, increases in capital will contribute to increases in productivity, which increases per capita GDP (Solow 1956). In Nigeria’s case, the opposite occurs, where in our period there is an increase in GFCF, but GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) falls according to Bolt and Zanden (2023). GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) fell 5.34% while GFCF and its share increased (African Development Bank Group 2023; Bolt and Zanden 2023). This prevents us from aligning the country with the model, as per capita GDP (PPPadjusted) does not trend with capital formation. However, Nigeria’s share of GFCF as a percentage of GDP at PPP fell by 8.61% in the available data between 2013 and 2019, which follows the same decline for per capita GDP (PPP-adjusted), and its share (University of Groningen and University of California, Davis 2019). Applying the model when comparing GFCF and its share to per capita GDP (PPP-adjusted) yields unapplicable results, but when GFCF’s share is PPP-adjusted, we can find evidence of the model working to predict growth.
In the period from 2013 to 2023, Nigeria’s capital accumulation has significantly expanded, going beyond world averages, indicating an increase in the nation’s physical and monetary capital with the aim of improving its growth. Additionally, increased gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and its share of GDP have not yielded a similar trend in GDP per capita, but it does follow the share of GFCF as a percentage of GDP at PPP, as predicted in the Solow model.



Nigeria’s human capital is generally perceived as subpar, with a high population of 237.5 million; there is potential for the nation to benefit in human productivity (Statista 2025). According to the World Bank Group, 2023, Human Capital Index (HCI) is the productivity of an individual by the age of 18, with their education, skills and health. This report examines Nigeria’s current efforts in education and the resulting workforce to assess the nation’s position in managing and developing its human capital.





Although Nigeria has a population advantage, it underperforms in HCI inputs. By 2024, Nigeria’s HCI reached 0.42, indicating that Nigerians born that year will be 42% productive by age 18, while the world average is 0.65, ranking Nigeria 163rd in the world (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA) 2024). Additionally, the average years of schooling in Nigeria is 7.2 while the world’s is 8.9, resulting in adult literacy rates of 62% in the country and 87.3% worldwide (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA) 2024). Nigeria falls behind in cultivating productive individuals compared to the world standards, and this shows that challenges are hindering it from leveraging its human capital.
Education is a key component of HCI, and in 2025, Nigeria will spend 7% of its fiscal budget on education, well below UNESCO’s recommendation of 15% to 20% (Shehu and Onunwa 2025). Due to lower funding in this sector, Nigeria experiences shortages of school supplies and teachers, which prevent students from continuing their schooling and lead to fewer education years (Shehu and Onunwa 2025). However, there are foreign parties such as the World Bank Group that have committed to providing additional funds for Nigeria’s educational sector through the “HOPE-EDU program,” which will donate US$500 million (Nasir and Laushi 2025). Although the nation struggles to prioritise adolescent skills, its trajectory for growth could improve if its governance leverages external aid to its advantage.
While Nigeria works to improve its educational investment, its adult literacy rate remains low at 62% due to a poor educational system, with an additional discrepancy of a 20.4% difference between men and women in 2021 (Countryeconomy.com 2024). This impact is seen in the workforce’s productivity, as the nation faces a surplus of skilled and low-skilled individuals who cannot acquire further skills (World Bank 2025). The major gap between genders highlights the inequality in education, where women face barriers to entering the workforce or improving their skills. With less emphasis on women’s contributions, Nigeria’s growth potential is stagnated by a low-skilled workforce.
Nigeria is a nation that can leverage its large population to increase productivity; however, it faces shortcomings in producing individuals who can contribute to its economic growth. Weakened by a poor education system, many adults lack the necessary skills for efficient work, with women being sidelined. The nation’s low HCI is a culmination of these facts, but with aid and adequate institutions, this can be improved.



Nigeria’s financial system is a mixture of traditional formal banking and informal nonregulated services, according to the Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) (2024). While there is a variety of options, wealth gaps and gender inequality persist, which leave many financially excluded. According to the World Bank Group (2023), the financial inclusion rate is the percentage of adults who have access to formal or informal financial services. This report examines Nigeria’s financial exclusion and inclusion, how its population fares in this state and how its government addresses the issues.





The Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) (2024) credits formal bank market competition, increased mobile phone usage and urbanisation for affecting financial access in Nigeria. This has led to 64% of adult Nigerians being formally financially included and 74% with the additional informal means by 2023 (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). This is an increase from 68% in 2020, resulting in fewer people being financially excluded (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Although only 26% of adult Nigerians are financially excluded, this still accounts for 28.9 million people, mostly in rural areas and dependents such as women (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024).
As a result, Nigerians, many of whom live in the northern parts of the country, face barriers to financial well-being due to limited accessibility (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). While only 17% of urban residents are excluded, 37% of rural residents are excluded, which was a 2% increase from 35% in 2020, despite the national increase in services (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Due to increased urbanisation in Nigeria, formal banking services focus their attention on urban cities, ignoring rural areas, and this is evident in the agricultural sector, where small businesses face high barriers to accessing formal start-up funds (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). Due to a lack of formal services, informal services, which include connections and high-interest credit providers, are heavily relied on to provide financial needs (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024).
To address these issues, the Central Bank of Nigeria implemented the National Financial Inclusion Strategy in 2012, which aimed to reduce the exclusion rate to 20% by 2020. Despite not reaching the target, the exclusion rate is 26% by 2023, a significant decrease from 40% when the policy was first enacted (Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA) 2024). This was achieved through incentivizing competition in the banking sector to bring in a wider range of services, providing infrastructure in telecommunications to increase mobile phone usage for digital financial offerings and introducing services for dependents like women through micro-financing (Central Bank of Nigeria).
Nigeria’s mixed financial sector shows considerable promise, as evidenced by its progress in expanding financial accessibility through policy. There is an incentive for competition in the financial and technology sectors that aid financial inclusion. However, dependents such as women and rural residents continue to be excluded, which shows areas where improvement is needed.

title: Voter Turnout by Province
text:
Elections Canada is responsible for ensuring democratic standards are met in Canadian elections. It also publishes data on past elections, including election results, voter turnout, and voter demographic characteristics. This data can be used for multiple purposes in analysing the political landscape of Canada, such as in Elections Canada’s own summary reports comparing past elections. Since the data is public, we can conduct our own analyses. This short paper uses voting data from the 45th general election in 2025 to compare turnout between two provinces of choice, and discusses how demographic differences may explain the gap.
The data used here was retrived from Statistics Canada (2026), but it can also be downloaded from Elections Canada’s web portal.

title: Voter Turnout by Province
text:
National Turnout








Figure 1





What is Voter Turnout? Voter turnout is calculated as the total number of people who cast a ballot divided by the total number of people within a province who were eligible to do so, resulting in a proportion of eligible voters who voted (Statistics Canada 2026).
Figure 1 shows average voter turnout from the 45th general election in 2025, and shows that all provinces except Northwest Territories and Nunavut had turnout greater than 50%. This means most eligible voters in nearly every province cast a ballot, with Northwest Territories and Nunavut as the exceptions. According to Elections Canada (2026), this is an improvement in the overall turnout from the previous 44th general election by 6.4 percantage points.
For our comparison, we chose British Columbia, a relatively high turnout province, to compare against Nunavut, which had the lowest turnout in this election.

title: Voter Turnout by Province
text:
British Columbia Vs Nunavut








Figure 2





Figure 2 shows voter turnout from the last election for just these two provinces. British Columbia’s turnout was 63.28%, while Nunavut’s was 30.5%. They differ by 32.78%, making British Columbia’s turnout 2.07 times higher than Nunavut’s. With this gap established, we can now look at demographic differences between the provinces to help explain it.

Why does voter turnout vary between British Columbia and Nunavut?








Figure 3





Before answering this question, it’s worth noting that there could be many reasons for the turnout gap between these provinces, and our data limits us to a few well-supported explanations. Our dataset only captures turnout, location, age, and gender, so we examine those variables to see whether they help explain the difference.
Figure 3 shows turnout by age and gender for both provinces. We again see that British Columbia has substantially higher turnout overall. The 65 to 74 years age group has the highest turnout in British Columbia, while in Nunavut the 75 years and over have the highest turnout. Both provinces have their lowest turnout in the 18 to 24 years group. Every age group in British Columbia has at least a 40% turnout, but in Nunavut only the 45 and over groups reach that level. Turnout is similar across genders in both provinces.
This suggests age is the most significant factor behind this gap. Our data also shows that Nunavut has, on average, more eligible voters aged 18 to 34 than British Columbia does. However, Figure 3 shows that younger voters are less likely to vote in Nunavut, and while British Columbia follows the same age pattern, its overall turnout remains higher across every age bracket. This suggests that motivation to vote increases with age in both provinces, but some other systematic or cultural differences affect turnout within age groups. One possible explanation is that British Columbia residents may feel a greater sense of agency over or involvement in the federal government than residents of Nunavut do, though this is a guess and would need further research.

title: Voter Turnout by Province
text:
Conclusion
This paper showed that Elections Canada makes data on federal general elections public, allowing analysts to identify and report on turnout trends. Using turnout data from the 45th general election in 2025, we found that most of the nation’s eligible voters participated, with Northwest Territories and Nunavut as exceptions. Comparing British Columbia and Nunavut showed that British Columbia has substantially higher turnout, and that differences in age composition were the most significant factor that could explain the gap, suggesting systematic or cultural differences within age groups may be driving the phenomenon.
